props.title: Broken Arrow

sections.content: John Woo's Broken Arrow marked a crucial moment in 90s action cinema, bringing Hong Kong-style balletic violence to mainstream American audiences. Following the success of Hard Target (1993), Woo refined his signature style - dual-wielding guns, slow-motion doves, and operatic action sequences - while working with a bigger budget and star John Travolta at his charismatic peak. The film's nuclear weapon heist plot reflected growing post-Cold War anxieties, similar to contemporaries like Crimson Tide (1995) and The Rock (1996).

sections.content: Christian Slater's straight-arrow pilot provides the perfect foil to Travolta's scenery-chewing villain Deakins, establishing a template that Woo would perfect in Face/Off (1997). The desert setting allows for spectacular action pieces that combine military hardware with Woo's signature stylized violence. This approach influenced later desert-set action films like Mission: Impossible - Ghost Protocol (2011) and Sahara (2005).

The film's handling of nuclear weapons as a terrorist threat preceded similar plots in True Lies (1994) and The Peacemaker (1997), reflecting Hollywood's shift from Cold War narratives to rogue actor scenarios. The technical authenticity of military hardware and procedures, while not perfect, set a standard for mid-90s action thrillers like Executive Decision (1996). SUBHEAD: John Woo's American Evolution

sections.content: Broken Arrow represents the middle phase of Woo's Hollywood period, between the modest success of Hard Target (1993) and the big-budget excess of Mission: Impossible II (2000). The film maintains his Hong Kong signatures while adapting to American studio requirements, creating a hybrid style that influenced action directors like Robert Rodriguez in Desperado (1995) and Antoine Fuqua in Replacement Killers (1998).
